segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to the assembly of God that is in Corinth, to those made holy in Christ Jesus, called to be holy ones, together with all who in every place call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I always thank my God for you because of the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for in every way you were made rich in him, in all speech and all knowledge,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as the testimony about Christ was firmly established among you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you lack no gift as you eagerly await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He will also keep you firmly established to the end, blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: God is faithful, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I urge you, brothers and sisters, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be knit together in the same mind and the same judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Chloe’s people have made it clear to me, my brothers and sisters, that there are quarrels among you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I mean is this: each of you is saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” “I to Cephas,” “I to Christ.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Has Christ been divided up? Was it Paul who was crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am thankful that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no one can say that you were baptized into my name.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Well, I did also baptize the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to announce the good news, and not with wisdom of speech, so that the cross of Christ would not be emptied of its force.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of those who understand I will set aside.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Where is the wise person? Where is the scholar? Where is the debater of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of the world foolish?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not come to know God through wisdom, God was pleased, through the foolishness of the proclamation, to save those who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but we proclaim Christ crucified: a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings, and what is weak in God is stronger than human beings.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Consider your calling, brothers and sisters: not many of you were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise, and God chose what is weak in the world to shame what is strong,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and God chose what is lowborn in the world and what is despised, the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no flesh may boast before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is from him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and holiness and redemption,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that, as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always recognizable.

The verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy,” the same word that appears as “holy ones” later in this verse, and a Greek reader would have heard the link. Most translations use “sanctified”; the meaning is not in dispute, only the choice of English.

The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints,” but that word now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not what Paul means.
The Greek says only “theirs and ours.” Most interpreters attach this to “Lord,” as here. It could instead attach to “place” (“in every place, theirs and ours”).

The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is addressing the whole community. Older translations have “brethren” or “brothers”; many recent ones use “brothers and sisters.”

notes.phrase: “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” “I to Cephas,” “I to Christ.”
notes.note: Cephas is the Aramaic name of Peter. Apollos was a teacher who worked in Corinth after Paul had founded the community there. Whether “I belong to Christ” was the slogan of a fourth group or is Paul’s own retort to the other three is disputed; the text here treats it as a fourth slogan, which is the more common view.

Many manuscripts read “I thank God” or “I thank my God.” The SBLGNT follows the shorter reading without “God,” found in some of the earliest witnesses; the longer forms are probably scribal expansions.

The Greek verb was an ordinary word for bringing or publicly announcing good news. “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a kind of book, so “good news” is used throughout; many modern translations do the same in places.

The word most likely refers here to the Jewish expert in the Scriptures, set beside the Greek “wise person.” The traditional “scribe” now suggests a copyist, whereas such a person was a trained interpreter and teacher. The line echoes Isaiah 33:18.

Older translations have “this world,” but the Greek is a time-word meaning an era. It reflects the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. “World” at the end of the verse is a different Greek word (kosmos). Most modern translations also have “age” here.

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples” and in the plural was the standard Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples; it is the same word translated “nations” elsewhere. Paul uses it interchangeably with “Greeks” in verses 22 and 24 as the counterpart to “Jews.”

The Greek is literally “according to flesh,” meaning as measured in ordinary human terms. The same word appears in verse 29, where “no flesh” is a Semitic idiom for “no human being” and has been kept.

notes.phrase: and righteousness and holiness and redemption
notes.traditional: and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption
notes.note: The Greek can be read as listing four things Christ became (wisdom, righteousness, holiness, redemption) or as explaining “wisdom” by the other three (“wisdom from God, that is, righteousness, holiness and redemption”). Many scholars favor the second reading; the text here keeps the looser “and” of the traditional rendering. “Holiness” translates a noun from the same family as “made holy” in verse 2, traditionally “sanctification.”

candidates.reason: The plural address recurs in every letter and translators split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so it needs one policy.
Frequent in the Gospels and Acts, where “scribe,” “scholar,” “expert in the Law” and “teacher of the law” are all plausible and should not vary by chapter.

candidates.rendering: by human standards (κατὰ σάρκα); flesh (πᾶσα σάρξ)
candidates.reason: Paul’s uses of “flesh” range from the body to human standards to the sinful sphere, and the choice between “flesh” and paraphrase must be consistent across the letters.
Recurs in Romans and 1 Corinthians 12, where “gift,” “spiritual gift” and “gift of grace” compete and the link to χάρις may need to be signaled consistently.
The noun partner of ἁγιάζω (“make holy” in the register), traditionally “sanctification”; it should be fixed so that it matches the verb across Romans, 1 Thessalonians and Hebrews.
